C0.quote: a sequence of proposal-making rounds followed by a voting round
C0.note: Democratic procedures in which agenda-setters make proposals and citizens choose between them by majority/plurality vote; analysis of strategic agenda-setting and efficiency of the procedure.

C1.quote: we look for subgame-perfect Nash equilibria
C1.note: Main results characterise subgame-perfect equilibrium outcomes of procedures and evaluate them against utilitarian efficiency; agenda-setters' strategic proposal-making is analysed only through equilibrium, not as a separate incentive/manipulation result, so SB is not coded.

C2.1.value: votes / voting decision on proposals (proposal vs counter-proposal, or proposal vs status quo)
C2.1.quote: a voting decision for each pair of proposals

C2.2.quote: all citizens vote for one of the two proposals using majority
C2.2.note: Input is a single vote for one proposal (plurality rule, reducing to majority between two proposals); not a profile of pairwise comparisons or a majority relation, so OTH (single-choice vote).

C2.3.quote: differ with regard to the utility they obtain from the public project
C2.3.note: Benefits v_j in {Vw, Vl} and net utility u_j(pi) are held attitudes.

C2.4.loc: Sect. 3.4, p. 111; Sect. 5.1, p. 120; Appendix A, p. 123
C2.4.note: Voting decisions are a separate component of the equilibrium strategy profile, distinct from the utilities u_j; Appendix A derives voting behaviour from utility comparisons, and 'truthfully' presupposes that votes could differ from utilities.

C3.1.note: Voters always vote according to their utility between the two options; only agenda-setters' proposals are strategic.

C3.2.quote: as is standard, citizens vote as if they were pivotal
C3.2.note: Also Sect. 5.1, p. 120: 'citizens vote truthfully and non-strategically'.

C3.3.quote: as is standard, citizens vote as if they were pivotal
C3.3.note: Only appeal to standard practice; no specific citation or argument.

C4.1.note: C2.2 = OTH only; none of RANK/WEAK/APPR/DICH/PAIR, so the applicability condition is not met.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.quote: the utilitarian welfare measure associated with
C5.1.note: Efficiency/social optimality defined via utilitarian welfare and used in all propositions (types 1-3 inefficiencies).

C5.2.note: Welfare is computed from benefits v_j, subsidies and taxes, i.e. held utilities, not from votes.

VOT.quote_behav: citizens vote as if they were pivotal
VOT.note: Citizens' votes are fixed by utility comparison between the two options; Sect. 5.1, p. 120 also says 'citizens vote truthfully and non-strategically'. Agenda-setters are citizens too but are coded under CAN.

CAN.quote_behav: Agenda-setters are selfish and make proposals to maximize their utility
CAN.quote_info: identities of winners and losers and the public project’s parameters are common
CAN.note: Agenda-setters (ASw, ASl) who make proposals are coded as proponents of alternatives; the paper itself reinterprets them as policy-motivated candidates (Sect. 2, p. 108).

ORG.note: Procedure rules are fixed; no organiser acts within the game.

DES.quote_behav: planner should choose if s/he aims to maximize the utilitarian welfare
DES.quote_info: might also be unknown when the decision-making procedure needs to be chosen
DES.note: The benevolent planner's objective (utilitarian welfare) is stated explicitly (Definition 1), and Sect. 5.2 formalises the choice of procedure behind a veil of ignorance (Proposition 6), with parameters known only via distributions.

C7.1.quote: citizens vote as if they were pivotal
C7.1.note: CAN (agenda-setters) STRAT while VOT (citizens) NONSTRAT in the same equilibrium analyses.

C7.2.quote: as is standard, citizens vote as if they were pivotal
C7.2.note: Only an appeal to standard practice in prior work, with no argument for treating voters and agenda-setters differently; consistent with C3.3 = CONV.

C8.1.quote: we look for subgame-perfect Nash equilibria
C8.1.note: Games solved by backward induction; an informal cheap-talk announcement refinement is discussed in Sect. 4.3.

C8.2.quote: we look for subgame-perfect Nash equilibria

claims.quote: according to which minorities should have the first say
this result can help justify the use of procedures in democracy
provides novel theoretical support for the application of rules in democracies

C9.1.note: Claims about which procedure democracies should use (minority proposes first).

C9.2.quote: Agenda-setters are selfish and make proposals to maximize their utility
C9.2.note: Needed: agenda-setters strategic and selfish (stated p. 112); voters vote by their utilities (stated p. 111, 'vote as if they were pivotal'); complete information/common knowledge of valuations (stated p. 109); agenda-setters recognised by group membership (stated, discussed as caveat Sect. 4.1); welfare defined on held utilities (stated p. 110).

C10.1.loc: Sect. 1; Sect. 3 (Model); Sect. 5; Sect. 6 (Conclusion); Appendix A
C10.1.note: No statement that the procedure is studied only as a function of submitted inputs.

C1.reason: The agenda-setters' incentives are analysed only within equilibrium characterisations (EQ), with no separate result on manipulation or strategyproofness that would warrant SB.

C2.2.reason: Each citizen casts a single plurality/majority vote for one proposal, which is not a pairwise-comparison profile or majority relation as PAIR denotes.

C2.4.reason: Votes are modelled as equilibrium actions distinct from utilities u_j (separate objects, behaviour derived in Appendix A), so the paper treats input and held attitude as separate rather than equating them.

C4.1.reason: With C2.2 coded OTH the applicability condition for C4.1 fails.

C6.DES.reason: The paper explicitly states the planner's welfare objective and formally models the choice of procedure in Sect. 5.2 and Proposition 6, meeting the DES condition.

C7.2.reason: The only justification is the appeal 'as is standard' to prior practice, which is a convention/citation-type reference rather than an argument, matching CITE (consistent with C3.3 = CONV).
